newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai govt delays finance, property sector decrees.
newsitem.headline: Thai govt delays finance, property sector decrees.

text.p: Thailand on Monday delayed its plan to issue urgent measures to shore up its ailing finance and property sectors, saying the government needed more time to study the steps.

Deputy Finance Minister Thawatvong Na Chiangmai told reporters a plan for the government to approve five decrees to help lift the two troubled sectors would not be ready for cabinet consideration on Tuesday.
He said new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya asked for time to study the issues.
"It's a question of timing when to bring the decrees to the cabinet for consideration. It would most likely be taken up at next week's cabinet meeting," a government source told Reuters.

Government officials said earlier the cabinet was expected to approve the special royal decrees on guidelines for merging cash-strapped finance firms and on government roles in refinancing property loans extended by financial institutions.
Analysts had said the planned decrees could lift short term market sentiment, but in the long run there were question marks, particularly over mergers.

"I don't think these decrees would have much impact whether they are adopted this week or next. They are at relatively lower priority than renewed speculation about the baht and the upcoming figures from the central bank on Thursday," said Thanawat Pachimkul of Seamico Securities Plc.
"The decrees would help the finance sector but any mergers would take time anyway. It does not make much difference whether they are enforced this week or next," he added.

The proposed decrees include new laws on securitisation and a secondary mortgage corporation through which the state-run Government Savings Bank would buy property loans and assets from finance firms facing cashflow problems and resell them as securities.
Government officials said the decrees would probably include clearer guidelines on Thailand's recent moves to control offshore supply of its baht and curb market attacks on its currency.

Thailand's 91 finance firms have faced a severe liquidity crunch arising from high non-performing loans, shaky confidence in their stability, and prolonged high financing costs in the Thai money market.

Finance firms have paid an average interest rate of more than 20 percent for their short-term funding for several months with no quick relief in sight. The central bank has asked finance companies to cut deposit rates, the Thai Finance Companies Association said on Monday.

Most finance and securities companies suffered heavy first quarter losses and their positions are expected to worsen -- or stay the same -- for the rest of 1997, due to a prolonged slump of the Thai stock market which has lost about 60 percent of its value in the past year.
Analysts said central bank officials, in a move to expedite mergers among small finance firms, last month floated a warning that the Bank of Thailand may let uncooperative firms fold.
They said actual finance corporate mergers would be time-consuming as negotiations and corporate asset assessment need at least 100-150 days to be concluded.

"Medium or small finance firms would have no synergy to gain and few incentives to merge. The finance sector probably has only about five strong companies viewed as good merger leaders but they would likely ask the government to take care of the non-performing loans of small firms being taken in," an industry analyst said.

The analyst said with sufficient incentives including new bank licences, each of the five big finance companies could merge with six to seven smaller ones. This scenario would trim the sector down to 55-60 companies.
